title: Llívia, the Spanish town inside France
hook: A Spanish town sits entirely inside France because it was not a village.
peek: In 1659 Spain agreed to hand France 33 villages in the Pyrenees. Llívia had a royal charter making it a town, so it stayed Spanish, and today it sits wholly surrounded by French land.
lede: The Treaty of the Pyrenees in 1659 ended a long war between France and Spain and moved the border to the mountains. A follow-up agreement in 1660 gave France 33 villages in the Cerdanya valley. Llívia had been granted the status of a town by Emperor Charles V, so it was not counted as a village and stayed Spanish.

bullets.text: Llívia covers about 13 square kilometres and lies a short drive from the main border at Puigcerdà. It is a full part of Catalonia, in Spain, with Spanish schools, police and number plates.

To reach the rest of Spain, residents use a road that crosses a short stretch of France. For centuries its status was argued over, and it was agreed that traffic between Llívia and Spain could pass freely.
Llívia keeps one of the oldest pharmacies in Europe, said to date from the early 1400s. Its painted jars and old remedies are now displayed in the town museum.
